questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I chose Boston because I have long been fascinated by the United States as both a cultural and political space. Studying in the US is normally associated with extremely high tuition fees, making it inaccessible for most international students. This exchange opportunity therefore represented a unique chance to experience an American university environment without the otherwise prohibitive financial burden.
Furthermore, Boston is one of the leading academic hubs on the East Coast and is widely recognized as a center of knowledge, research, and intellectual innovation. With its concentration of world-class universities and a vibrant academic community, the city offers an exceptional environment for learning and personal development. For me, this made Boston the ideal destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I would rate my overall experience a 10 out of 10. During my stay, I had the opportunity to travel extensively, which allowed me to explore different parts of the United States and gain a much deeper understanding of the country’s cultural and regional diversity. I also rented a house together with four other girls from around the world, and this international living environment became one of the highlights of my stay. We formed close friendships, and I truly feel that I have gained friends for life.
Academically, the level and structure differed from what I am used to at home, and in general the academic demands were somewhat lower. However, I was aware of this before going, and therefore it did not negatively influence my overall experience. Instead, it allowed me to focus more on cultural immersion, personal development, and building an international network.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Finding the information I needed prior to and upon arrival was very easy. The university was highly responsive and provided clear guidance throughout the entire process, which made it straightforward to prepare for my stay. Their communication was quick, and they offered extensive orientation materials that helped me understand both administrative procedures and practical aspects of student life.
I did experience some challenges related to the visa process, but this seemed to be a common issue for many international students. Despite this, the overall availability and clarity of information from the university significantly eased the transition.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Upon arrival, I received extensive assistance from the university. Their exchange team is truly excellent (its a really rich college :)) and ensured that international students felt supported from the very beginning. They provided clear guidance during orientation, helped with practical matters, and made themselves available for any questions or concerns. This level of support created a smooth transition into both academic life and everyday living in Boston.

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Finding off-campus housing took some time, as the market in Boston is competitive and options disappear quickly. However, I would highly recommend asking the university for the QR code to the group for all incoming students. This platform made it much easier to connect with others who were also searching for housing. Through the group, I ended up meeting four other girls, and together we rented a house via a housing portal approved by the university, which added an extra layer of security and reliability. Overall, while the process required patience, using student networks and university-recommended platforms proved to be the most effective approach.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Future exchange students should be aware that living off campus can be both a better and more affordable option compared to on-campus housing. During my stay, I saw the on-campus facilities, and many students were placed in crowded rooms while also paying significantly higher rent. In addition, living on campus requires purchasing a mandatory meal plan, which I found to be of low quality and not good value for money. Off-campus housing, by contrast, offers more space, greater independence, and often a better overall living environment. Students should also be aware that some dorm buildings have strict access control, including police presence at certain entrances for first-year students. For those seeking flexibility, comfort, and a more authentic experience of the city, off-campus living is a strong alternative. If you have the opportunity to live on Foster Street THEN DO IT.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course registration process was very intuitive, and the university provided a large amount of helpful information in advance. There is no need to stress about choosing the perfect courses beforehand, as it is quite easy to make changes once you arrive on campus. Advisors are accessible and supportive, and the system is flexible for exchange students. However, getting my courses pre-approved at the University of Copenhagen was more challenging. KU required extensive documentation, which the university in Boston either could not or would not provide before arrival. This made the pre-approval process somewhat risky, as final confirmation often depended on information only available once you were physically at the university.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Before the semester began, I received extensive information by email, guiding me to the university’s online platform, which functions similarly to Canvas/Absalon. Through this system, I created my initial course “table,” selecting the classes I planned to take. It is important to be aware of several rules when registering: exchange students may take a maximum of 16 credits, courses are not allowed to overlap in schedule, and it is not permitted to take all four courses within the same department. Although the initial registration requires attention to these details, the table can be easily adjusted once you arrive on campus. Advisors are helpful, and the system is flexible, ensuring that students can finalise their schedules without unnecessary stress.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Mailing them and reading the instructions send out.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Overall, I was partially successful in registering for the classes I had planned. I was able to secure a course that fulfilled the requirement for DAK3, which was my primary academic priority. However, the university removed the course on European Politics shortly before the semester started, which created a significant challenge. I attempted to find an equivalent replacement, but the University of Copenhagen was not willing to approve any of the alternative courses offered in Boston. As a result, I ended up taking three electives along with DAK3, while completing the European Politics course online from home. Although this solution worked in practice, it was somewhat stressful to coordinate and required additional planning.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My main advice to future exchange students is to stay open-minded when it comes to course selection. The academic structure and teaching style differ significantly from what we are used to at the University of Copenhagen, so it is helpful to approach the process with flexibility. Courses may change, be removed, or require additional documentation, and it is likely that you will need to reprioritise or revise your initial plans. It is important not to let these adjustments overshadow the overall experience. With proper planning and a willingness to adapt, the registration process becomes much more manageable, and students can still create an academically valuable and personally enriching study programme.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, I was satisfied with the academic programme, although it differed significantly from what I am used to at the University of Copenhagen. The coursework was generally much easier, and I did not feel as academically challenged in a traditional sense. However, I was stimulated in a different way by gaining insight into how American students think, participate, and approach academic work. This cultural and pedagogical contrast was highly valuable and broadened my academic perspective.
In terms of structure, the courses tended to prioritise quantity over depth. While the syllabus was somewhat lighter, there were numerous quizzes, presentations, and smaller assignments that required continuous attention and often took considerable time.
For future students, I would strongly recommend taking a course with -NAME REDACTED-  if possible. He is a French professor with a background from Cornell, and the academic level in his classes is notably higher and intellectually engaging.

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: One of the most striking differences in the academic level was the pedagogical approach. The system places a stronger emphasis on memorisation, personal political opinions, and active participation rather than on developing an objective, theoretically grounded academic understanding. Discussions often encouraged students to express their viewpoints, but not necessarily to anchor them in broader theoretical frameworks or methodological rigor. As a result, it sometimes felt as though the classes remained on the lower steps of the theoretical “ladder.” While students engaged actively, the courses rarely moved into deeper conceptual analysis or advanced theoretical synthesis of the kind typically expected at KU. This difference does not make the courses less valuable; rather, it highlights a distinct academic culture where engagement and opinion formation are prioritised over theoretical abstraction. To me its wild paying that much and the recieve that little in terms of academic development.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university offered a wide range of clubs and sports activities, and at first glance the extracurricular environment appeared very active. However, many of the clubs were relatively superficial in their engagement, and it was my experience that American students were generally not particularly interested in integrating exchange students into their social groups (I have heard thats an east-coast thing and i found that to be true). While opportunities existed, it often required significant initiative to become meaningfully involved. In terms of sports, the university had an extensive athletic programme, but many of the sports clubs were effectively closed to exchange students. This is because several teams operate as semi-professional organisations, where athletes receive compensation, making them inaccessible to regular students. As a result, although the campus seemed vibrant and full of activities, the practical opportunities for exchange students to participate fully were more limited than expected.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sport, language clubs etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend that future exchange students consider joining the rugby team (I did not play rugby before going), as this was one of the most enjoyable and welcoming environments I experienced. The team was down-to-earth, inclusive, and provided a great opportunity to meet students outside the typical exchange circles.
The university’s outdoor club is also an excellent option. Through this group, I was able to go on hikes with local students in various states, which offered a unique chance to explore the natural landscapes of the East Coast while also building meaningful connections.
Additionally, I participated in a prison education programme, where students visited correctional facilities to teach. This was an extraordinarily enriching and eye-opening experience—both academically and personally. It offered a rare opportunity to engage with social issues in a direct and impactful way, and I would strongly recommend it to anyone interested in community engagement or criminal justice.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would strongly encourage future exchange students to take advantage of the many travel opportunities available on the East Coast. During my stay, I visited New York, Canada, and Puerto Rico — and all three trips were truly fantastic experiences. Each destination offered something completely different: the cultural and architectural intensity of New York, the natural beauty and welcoming atmosphere in Canada, and the unique Caribbean culture and climate in Puerto Rico.
Travelling during the semester provided valuable breaks from academic life and allowed me to experience the broader cultural diversity of the region, which greatly enriched my exchange experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
For me, adjusting to the local culture was relatively easy. I quickly found a large group of wonderful people and ended up forming what felt like a small European “bubble” within the US, which made the transition smooth and enjoyable. However, it became clear that experiences varied significantly among exchange students. Some students from Spain, France, and other countries found it more challenging to adapt. Several struggled with the academic structure, which differs markedly from many European systems, while others found the cost of living overwhelming or encountered difficulties with on-campus housing.
Overall, while the adjustment process depends heavily on personal expectations and circumstances, my own experience was positive due to the strong social network I built early on. - Boston is really save and kinda European, so its very nice.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
What I appreciated most about the culture in the United States was its complexity and diversity. The country is full of contrasts—socially, politically, and culturally—which makes it an incredibly dynamic place to experience. The U.S. offers countless opportunities, but it also contains tensions and challenges that are important to witness firsthand. Experiencing these dynamics up close gave me a much deeper understanding of American society than I could have gained from a distance.
Being on exchange provided a unique opportunity to explore this multifaceted culture in an immersive way, and it confirmed for me how valuable international study experiences can be in broadening one’s perspective.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Consider what kind of cultural experience you want.
If your goal is to make American friends and truly challenge your worldview, I would recommend considering an exchange in the Midwest. Although I loved Boston, I sometimes wished I had chosen a location where it might have been easier to integrate more deeply into American everyday life.

2. Save up before you go.
Boston is an expensive city (and the college is a college for some of the richest kids in MA), and having some financial flexibility makes a significant difference. Saving up beforehand allows you to fully enjoy the experience — whether that means travelling, joining activities, or simply participating in social events without stress.

3. Say yes to everything.
The exchange experience goes by incredibly fast, so take every opportunity that comes your way. Even the less successful or challenging moments become valuable experiences in hindsight. Be proactive, invite others to join, and travel whenever you can — most people are happy to come along if someone takes the initiative.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the personal development it brought. Living abroad gave me a renewed sense of gratitude for my life at home, while also pushing me to grow in ways that would not have been possible otherwise. I met an incredible number of new people from all over the world, each contributing to broadening my perspective and challenging me socially, academically, and personally. Being placed in new environments and situations forced me to adapt, reflect, and step outside my comfort zone.
These experiences — from forming deep friendships to navigating unfamiliar systems — collectively made the exchange one of the most meaningful and transformative periods of my life.
The US is an amazing country.
